options: A signed set of query-string parameters granting time-limited, scoped access to a storage resource, without sharing an account key or creating an identity
A permanent password for a storage account
A type of managed identity
A billing plan for Azure Storage
questions.explain: SAS tokens grant scoped, expiring access purely through a signed URI — no identity or stored key exposure needed.

questions.q: What does the 'sig' parameter in a SAS token represent?
options: The cryptographic signature proving the token was generated by someone who had the account key
The name of the storage account
The file size limit for uploads
The user's email address
questions.explain: The signature is what actually authorizes the request, without the account key itself ever being exposed.

questions.q: What is the classic 'front end proxy' pattern SAS tokens enable?
options: A backend issues a short-lived SAS token, then the client talks directly to storage for the actual upload/download, without routing file traffic through the backend
The backend must always proxy every byte of file data itself
SAS tokens can only be used by backend services, never clients
Clients must always use a managed identity instead of a SAS token
questions.explain: This offloads the actual data transfer from the backend, letting the client interact with storage directly and securely.

questions.q: When would you use a SAS token instead of a managed identity?
options: For a client you don't fully control, or access that should genuinely expire — like a browser upload or a link shared with an external partner
Only for Azure Functions and VMs, never external clients
SAS tokens and managed identities are always interchangeable with no difference
Only when working with Azure Databricks specifically
questions.explain: Managed identities suit resources you control with ongoing access needs; SAS tokens suit external or temporary access.

questions.q: Why is a short expiry time important for a SAS token?
options: Because revoking a SAS token early generally requires rotating the account key (which invalidates every token signed with it), so minimizing the window matters
Short expiry has no real security benefit
SAS tokens automatically renew themselves, so expiry doesn't matter
Long expiry times make tokens more secure, not less
questions.explain: Since permissions and expiry are baked into the signed token, keeping expiry short limits the damage if a token leaks.
